title: Hardness of coloring 2-dicolorable digraphs with any fixed number of colors
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 4\), is it NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions to distinguish digraphs with dichromatic number at most 2 from digraphs with dichromatic number greater than k?
why: Tests how much approximation helps when searching for a partition into acyclic subgraphs. Constant-color hardness would establish a strong obstruction even when an optimal two-part partition is promised to exist.
status_note: Published Question 2, its following conjectural sentence and the coloring model checked through 11 September 2026; the May 2026 full-version record and later searches yielded no matching resolution for every fixed k.

progress.text: The ICALP paper supplies a \(2\sqrt{n}\)-color algorithm, records known three-color hardness and asks about every larger constant palette.

importance.reason: Tests constant-factor approximation hardness for partitioning a digraph into acyclic sets under a two-colorability promise, a structural counterpart of hard coloring problems. The existing numerical score is retained during formulation review.

sentences: A dicoloring partitions a directed graph into color classes containing no directed cycle.
The input is promised to admit two colors, but that coloring is not supplied.
The source conjecturally asks whether producing any fixed larger number of colors remains NP-hard.
Its polynomial-time algorithm uses a number of colors growing as the square root of the vertex count.
Settling the constant-color hardness claim would clarify whether a bounded relaxation of the optimum can overcome the search difficulty.

definitions: A digraph \(D=(V,A)\) has labeled vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\), no loops, and at most one arc in each direction between distinct vertices; opposite arcs are allowed. Its binary encoding explicitly lists vertices and arcs. A directed cycle has at least two distinct vertices \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{\ell}\) and arcs \(v_{i}\to v_{i+1}\), with indices modulo \(\ell\). A k-dicoloring is a map \(c:V\to \{1,\ldots ,k\}\) such that each color class induces an acyclic digraph, equivalently no directed cycle is monochromatic. The dichromatic number is the least k admitting such a map. The promise problem for k accepts inputs with dichromatic number at most 2 and rejects those with dichromatic number greater than k; inputs with values \(3,\ldots ,k\) are outside the promise. The NP-hardness claim means that for each fixed k there is a deterministic algorithm \(R_{k}\) and constants \(c_{k},C_{k}\) such that, on a 3-CNF formula F of bit length \(N, R_{k}\) outputs a digraph in time at most \(C_{k}(N+1)^{c}_{k}\), with satisfiable F mapped to the accepting side and unsatisfiable F mapped to the rejecting side. A 3-CNF is a conjunction of clauses of at most three literals, each a variable or its negation. The reduction and its polynomial may depend on k, but not on F or N; k is not an input-size parameter. A promised coloring algorithm is given the graph without a 2-coloring and must return a valid k-dicoloring. A gap reduction of the stated kind rules out such a polynomial-time algorithm unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), since validity of an output coloring can be checked in polynomial time.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated NP-hardness for every fixed \(k\ge 4\), or refute that universal hardness assertion. A polynomial-time k-coloring algorithm for some fixed k would contradict the claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). Hardness for \(k=3\), bounds for a growing number of colors, or hardness without the two-colorability completeness promise do not suffice.

context_blocks.title: A color class may contain directed edges
context_blocks.text: In a directed path \(u\to v\to w\), all three vertices may receive the same color because there is no directed cycle. In a directed triangle \(u\to v\to w\to u\) they may not all receive the same color. This differs from ordinary graph coloring, which forbids any monochromatic edge.

context_blocks.title: The input has a good coloring but does not reveal it
context_blocks.text: The promise guarantees that two acyclic color classes exist. The algorithm is allowed more colors to make the search easier. If the two-coloring itself were supplied, the task would already be solved; it is deliberately absent from the input.

context_blocks.title: The source’s proposed hardness target
context_blocks.text: The paper asks about every constant k greater than three and then suggests that the problem may be NP-hard for every such k, as in a related hypergraph setting. This card adopts that explicit conjectural gap-hardness formulation, making the intended yes/no proposition reviewable.

context_blocks.title: Known algorithms still use a growing palette
context_blocks.text: The paper gives a polynomial-time algorithm using at most \(2\sqrt{n}\) colors for a 2-dicolorable n-vertex digraph. It also records three-color hardness, even on tournaments. Neither result answers whether any larger fixed palette changes the complexity on general digraphs.
